subject: BIM
author: Anthony Hammond
title: What Is BIM and Why Should You Care? (Developers)
subHeading: How coordinated information can reduce construction delays, avoid rework and protect the long-term value of your investment.
abstract: BIM is more than a 3D model. Discover how coordinated digital information can help developers reduce avoidable construction costs, improve project delivery and make buildings easier to operate and maintain.
body:
Building Information Modelling explained through the thing developers care about most: protecting the value of their investment.

## What is BIM?

When you invest millions in a building, you are paying for more than concrete, steel, mechanical systems and finishes. You are investing in an asset that needs to be constructed, operated and maintained for years to come.

Building Information Modelling (BIM) is an approach to managing a building’s information throughout its lifecycle. It brings together digital models, project data and coordinated processes so that the people designing, constructing and operating a building can work with reliable, relevant information.

**BIM is not simply about creating a 3D model.** It is about coordinating information to make better decisions, reduce avoidable problems and deliver a building that is easier to manage.

## The HVAC example: without BIM

Imagine you have commissioned a commercial building with a complex heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) system.

During construction, the mechanical contractor begins installing ductwork and equipment using the drawings available to them. But the structural design has changed, a beam occupies the same space as a duct run, and there is insufficient clearance to install or maintain an air-handling unit.

**The conflict is discovered on site.**

Work stops while the teams investigate. Engineers revise the design, contractors wait for updated information, and installed work may need to be removed or modified. Labour is wasted, materials may be scrapped, and the construction programme risks falling behind.

These problems can be particularly expensive when one delayed activity prevents other trades from progressing.

The building is eventually completed, but the information problems may continue. Years later, the air-handling unit develops a fault. The facilities manager cannot easily find accurate equipment details, commissioning records or maintenance documentation. Someone must investigate the installation, track down records or survey the system before the repair can proceed.

**The developer can end up paying twice:** first for avoidable construction delays and rework, then for the consequences of incomplete or unreliable handover information.

## The HVAC example: with BIM

Now consider the same project using a well-planned BIM process.

The architectural, structural and mechanical models are federated into a coordinated digital view of the building. The team can review how the different systems fit together and identify potential clashes, access restrictions and installation problems before work reaches site.

For example, if a ventilation duct conflicts with a structural beam, the issue can be identified and resolved during design coordination rather than discovered when a contractor is ready to install it.

That early resolution can reduce rework, wasted labour, material costs and delays. It also helps different trades plan their work around coordinated information, reducing the risk of one team arriving on site only to find that the area is not ready.

BIM does not automatically find every conflict or guarantee a project finishes on time. The models must be sufficiently detailed, kept up to date and properly reviewed. But identifying problems earlier generally gives the team more options to resolve them before they become expensive site issues.

The benefits continue at handover. From the outset, the developer defines what information is needed to operate and maintain the building. Equipment identifiers, specifications, commissioning records and maintenance requirements can be collected, checked and organised as the project progresses.

When that air-handling unit eventually needs attention, the facilities manager has a better chance of accessing the right information without starting from scratch.

## Why should developers care?

Because the developer funds the project, carries significant financial exposure and ultimately owns the asset.

Federated information can help reduce avoidable construction delays and rework. Well-managed handover information can make the completed building easier and less expensive to operate. Together, these benefits can protect both the construction budget and the long-term value of the investment.

BIM is not about producing the most impressive digital model. It is about making sure the right people have the right information when they need it — from design and construction through to operation.

**If you are paying for the building, you should care about the process that helps deliver it efficiently and the information you receive when it is finished.**
